headline: One power trace of ML-KEM key generation on a Cortex-M4 cuts the standardised post-quantum key exchange's estimated attack cost by more than 140 bits, and Vahid Jahandideh's 937-byte change to how the sampler stores a number restores nearly all of it.

items.title: Negative capacitance amplifies the bandgap, not the surface potential
items.dek: Rahul Awale and five co-authors model a transistor whose ferroelectric gate amplifies the electric field that opens a bandgap in bilayer graphene rather than the channel potential, and compute a switching slope of 15 millivolts per tenfold change in current at 300 kelvin.
items.why_it_matters: Every negative-capacitance transistor so far has fought the same matching problem: the ferroelectric supplies gain only while its capacitance sits close to the semiconductor's, and a channel's capacitance moves as carriers fill it, so the gain drifts away exactly where the device is switching. Routing the amplification into the size of a bandgap instead of into a carrier density takes the channel out of that feedback loop, and it changes what a candidate channel material has to be good at — a large, field-tunable gap rather than a conveniently small density of states.
items.background_md: A transistor turns off by raising an energy barrier that carriers have to climb thermally. Their energies are spread by temperature according to Boltzmann statistics, so the current below threshold falls exponentially with barrier height, and at 300 kelvin it takes roughly 60 millivolts of gate swing to cut that current by a factor of ten. The number is a property of temperature rather than of fabrication, and it sets a floor under supply voltage: a logic gate needs several decades of on/off ratio, so it needs several times 60 millivolts of gate range, and switching energy scales with the square of that voltage.
items.deeper_md:
The modelled stack is bilayer graphene gated through Al₀.₅₅Sc₀.₄₅N. Bilayer graphene has no gap until a perpendicular field breaks the symmetry between its two sheets, and the gap then grows with the interlayer potential difference — the effect Kuzmenko and colleagues pinned down by fitting gate-modulated infrared reflectivity to a tight-binding model. The ferroelectric amplifies that interlayer potential rather than the carrier density, and the authors report the gate-voltage window needed to open the gap compressed 37-fold against a dielectric-gated control.

Everything here is simulation: a four-band tight-binding Hamiltonian with GW-corrected screening, a quasistatic Landau–Devonshire ferroelectric response, and ballistic Landauer–Büttiker transport. No device was built.

The limit is stated in the abstract. Room-temperature on/off ratio is only about 10², set by how big bilayer graphene's field-induced gap can get; logic wants 10⁵ or better. The swing improves to 2.5 mV/dec at 100 K, which is where any thermally limited number goes when you cool it.

Negative capacitance is itself disputed. Kittl and co-workers argue the capacitance-matching stabilisation these designs assume is "fundamentally flawed and unphysical", and that microscopic measurements show mixed ferroelectric domains rather than the uniform low-polarisation state the models require.

glossary.definition: The gate voltage needed to change drain current by a factor of ten. Thermal injection over a barrier puts a floor near 60 mV/decade on it at room temperature.

A ferroelectric biased where its polarisation falls as the applied field rises, so the voltage across it drops when charge is added; in series with a gate oxide the channel then sees more voltage than the gate supplies.
Extra capacitance arising from a channel's finite density of states. It sits in series with the gate oxide and shifts as the channel fills, which is what makes capacitance matching a moving target.
A thermodynamic description of a ferroelectric as a double-well free energy in polarisation; the barrier between the wells is the region where the differential capacitance is negative.

items.title: A substrate matched four ways: lattice, expansion, conduction, phonons
items.dek: MVS Chandrashekhar and two dozen co-authors grew single-crystal scandium diboride and report that it matches the lattice of Al₀.₅₅Ga₀.₄₅N while conducting like a metal at about 15 microhm-centimetres, which is what a vertical power transistor needs underneath it.
items.why_it_matters: A vertical power device conducts down through its substrate, so whatever resistance the substrate has is added in series with the device itself — the authors call that the factor limiting what an ultra-wide-bandgap channel can deliver. Making the substrate metallic removes the term; matching its lattice constant and its thermal expansion to the epitaxial layer is what lets that layer be grown thick enough to block kilovolts without cracking on cooldown. The fourth criterion is the one nobody normally lists: matching Debye temperature, so the two lattices share phonon modes and heat actually crosses the interface instead of reflecting off it.
items.background_md: A power transistor has to block a high voltage when off and pass current with little loss when on, and both demands land on the same drift layer. Widening the bandgap raises the electric field the material survives before avalanche, so an aluminium-rich AlGaN alloy blocks more volts per micrometre than GaN does. What the alloy cannot do is shed its own heat: its thermal conductivity sits well below GaN's, so a device built in it runs hotter for the same geometry, and the substrate underneath ends up doing much of the cooling as well as carrying the current.
items.deeper_md:
The crystals come from a laser-diode floating-zone furnace at about 1 mm/hr under boron-rich conditions, with a (002) rocking-curve width of 38 arcseconds — the paper's own yardstick is that this approaches commercial SiC and GaN substrate quality. Lattice-expansion measurements put the coefficient of thermal expansion near 5 ppm/K at AlGaN growth temperatures and the lattice match at Al₀.₅₅Ga₀.₄₅N. Resistivity runs 15 µΩ·cm at room temperature to 93 µΩ·cm at 773 K with a T² dependence, and the surface finishes at roughly 2.5 nm rms.

Two measured numbers disagree with theory and the authors say so. Thermal conductivity lands at 53 W/m·K, half the full first-principles value, and resistivity is about twice theoretical; both are attributed to scandium vacancies generated by the boron-rich growth. The 10–100× power-handling gain over GaN-on-SiC quoted in the abstract is a projection resting on engineered phonon bridges and polaritons at the interface, not a measured device.

The competing route is a conductive carbide. Zahn and co-workers, sharing authors with this paper, anneal TaC thin films in nitrogen to tune rock-salt Ta(C,N) across Al_xGa₁₋ₓN from x = 0.5 to 1, and find crystal quality and surface morphology degrade together at 1600 °C and above as secondary phases appear.

glossary.definition: One whose current flows from a top contact down through the epitaxial layer and out the back of the wafer, which puts the substrate in the current path and adds its resistivity to the device's on-resistance.
The angular range over which a crystal still diffracts X-rays, here 38 arcseconds. It measures how much the lattice planes tilt from place to place, so a narrow curve means little mosaic spread.
How much a material lengthens per kelvin, in parts per million. A film-substrate mismatch becomes stress on cooling from growth temperature, and then wafer bow or cracks.

The temperature set by the highest lattice vibration a crystal supports. Two materials with similar values have overlapping phonon spectra, which is what lets vibrational energy cross the interface between them.

items.fab_angle: Expansion mismatch shows up as wafer bow long before it shows up as a cracked film, and bow is measurable with equipment a teaching lab already has. Measure a bare wafer's curvature on the profilometer, put a film on it at temperature, measure again, and Stoney's equation turns the change in curvature into film stress — the same measurement that tells you whether a sputtered or grown layer will survive the next thermal step.

items.title: Floorsweeping makes every GPU a different chip, and schedulers notice
items.dek: Xiaoze Fan and ten co-authors measured that permanently disabling defective blocks for yield leaves each GPU with its own arrangement of working compute units, and that ignoring which ones you get costs up to 1.33 times performance variation between chips carrying the same part number.
items.why_it_matters: Yield harvesting has always been invisible above the driver: a part is sold as having some number of streaming multiprocessors, and software asks for that many rather than for particular ones. Two things break that abstraction at current die sizes. Which physical units survived testing differs from chip to chip, and the die is now big enough that cache and memory are split into partitions, so how far a unit sits from the data it wants becomes part of the allocation decision. A scheduler that chooses how many resources without choosing which is picking at random among options that differ measurably.
items.background_md: A large die is never fully functional. Defects land at random across a wafer, so a manufacturer designs in redundant blocks, permanently disables the ones that failed test, and sells the die in whatever bin its surviving count lands in. That practice is what keeps yield economic at reticle-scale dies, where a single killer particle would otherwise scrap the whole part. The consequence carried forward into the datacentre is that two chips on the same shelf, with the same name and the same advertised resource count, do not have the same set of physical resources working.
items.deeper_md:
The measured asymmetries come in two kinds. Compute topology: which units survived floorsweeping decides how an allocation maps onto the chip's clusters, and a topology-oblivious allocation produces up to 1.33× performance variation. Memory affinity: a remote access raises HBM latency by up to 67% and close to doubles L2 latency. The authors build lightweight probes that recover both per chip, then feed the map into existing fine-grained schedulers — improving mainstream kernels by up to 1.22×, multiplexed LLM inference by up to 14.3%, and removing the 1.33× spread.

Two independent measurements point the same way. Alpay and Basaran probed all 142 units of an NVIDIA L40 and found L2 hit latency spanning 222–339 cycles rather than one value near 279 — a 52% range, two-fold symmetric across two halves of 72 units, following the AD102 cluster layout. Alpay and Alpay report a Blackwell B200 as a two-die package with a 74/74 unit split and a 30-cycle, 15.5 ns cross-die penalty.

The caveat is structural: these maps are properties of an individual chip, not of a part number, so they have to be measured on the machine you are actually running on. That is precisely why the effect stayed hidden underneath the logical abstraction for so long.

glossary.definition: Permanently disabling blocks that failed test so a partly defective die can still be sold. It is why the set of working units differs from chip to chip even inside one product bin.
The block a GPU hands work to. A kernel launch asks for a count of them, and until this kind of probing nothing above the driver could ask for particular ones.
How many clock cycles a load takes when the data is found in the shared second-level cache. It is normally modelled as one number per chip, and on a partitioned die it is not.
Sorting finished dies into product tiers by how many redundant blocks survived and what clock they hold, which is how one design ships as several part numbers at several prices.

items.fab_angle: The redundancy scheme is a design decision made long before the wafer exists, and it has two edges. Fine repair granularity rescues more dies and therefore produces more distinct surviving topologies; coarse granularity keeps the shipped parts uniform and throws away more silicon per defect. Which side is right is set by the defect density the process actually achieves, so the same architecture wants a different redundancy plan on a mature line than on a ramping one.

items.title: Six FP4 multiplies instead of nine for one exact 8-bit integer product
items.dek: Shun-ichiro Hayashi and three co-authors found encodings that compute an exact 8-bit integer matrix product using six passes over the NVIDIA B200's four-bit floating-point units, down from the nine that the previously published splitting scheme required.
items.why_it_matters: A four-bit floating-point unit holds sixteen values and no wide integers at all, so using it for arithmetic that has to be exact means splitting each operand into digits it can represent and paying one full matrix multiply per pair of digits. That product count, not the clock rate, decides whether the fastest unit on the chip is worth pointing at work it was never designed for: at roughly double the throughput of the eight-bit format, nine multiplies is a wash and six is not. The same accounting will apply to every future format that trades mantissa bits for throughput.
items.background_md: Accelerators keep adding narrower number formats because a multiplier's area and energy grow faster than linearly with operand width, so halving the format roughly doubles what the same silicon delivers. Those formats are built for neural-network arithmetic, where being slightly wrong is tolerable. Work that cannot be wrong — dense linear algebra, scientific simulation — can still use them through a splitting trick: break each high-precision operand into several low-precision pieces chosen so that every pairwise product is exactly representable, then sum. The cost of the trick is the number of pieces squared, so it lives or dies on how few pieces are needed.
items.deeper_md:
The property being exploited is arithmetic, not architectural. Every FP4 value becomes an integer when doubled, and the resulting set S = {0, ±1, ±2, ±3, ±4, ±6, ±8, ±12} contains a representative of every residue class modulo 13 — so with carries, any integer can be written in base 13 using digits FP4 can store. The prior implementation, from the same group a month earlier, split each INT8 operand into three such limbs weighted (1, 13, 169) and multiplied them pairwise: 3 × 3 = 9 FP4 matrix multiplies per INT8 × INT8 product. Karatsuba and Toom–Cook do not rescue it as they stand, because their limb sums reach ±24 and fall outside S.

AWE lets the limb weights be arbitrary integers and the stored planes be linear combinations of limbs, recovering the exact product by summing the FP4 results under reconstruction coefficients. A search over those choices yields 6 products for INT8 × INT8 and 4 for INT4 × INT8. Working modulo m — the residue-number-system form used in Ozaki scheme II — the FP64 significand drops from 75 products to 59, and the crossover between residue and non-residue encodings sits near input width 15.

What the paper delivers is product counts and released encodings; the abstract claims no measured kernel speedup on a B200.

glossary.definition: A four-bit float with two exponent bits and one mantissa bit, so it represents sixteen values. Doubling every one of them gives an integer, which is the only reason exact integer work on it is possible.
General matrix-matrix multiply, the BLAS primitive accelerators are built around. It is the unit of cost here because each pair of split operands needs its own full pass over both matrices.
One low-precision digit of a split high-precision operand. The number of limbs squared is the number of matrix multiplies the emulation costs, which is why reducing it is the whole objective.

A family of methods that emulate high-precision matrix multiply on low-precision units by splitting inputs so each partial product is exactly representable, making the result error-free rather than merely close.

items.title: One power trace of ML-KEM key generation costs more than 140 bits
items.dek: Vahid Jahandideh reports that a single power trace of ML-KEM-768 key generation on an Arm Cortex-M4 — ML-KEM being the lattice key exchange standardised to replace Diffie–Hellman against quantum attack — leaks enough to drop the estimated attack cost from 2 to the 182 down to 2 to the 38.
items.why_it_matters: Key generation draws fresh randomness every run, so an attacker gets exactly one trace and cannot average noise away, which is why it has been treated as the easier half to protect. The leak here is not a secret-dependent branch or a table lookup. It comes from how the value is stored and what is done to it next: a signed 16-bit word gives away the sign, and multiplying by a public constant afterwards gives away the magnitude. The fix is correspondingly strange — store a random member of the same residue class instead of the small representative, and leave every later line of code untouched.
items.background_md: Lattice cryptography hides a secret inside a noisy linear system, and recovering it is a shortest-vector problem whose difficulty is quoted as the block size a lattice-reduction algorithm needs. Partial information moves that estimate directly: each reliable fact about a coefficient becomes a hint that can be folded into the lattice before reduction starts, shrinking the block size and with it the exponent in the running time. Power analysis is one way to collect hints, because the current a microcontroller draws depends on the bits it is moving. The question is never whether a device leaks, but whether what leaks amounts to enough hints.
items.deeper_md:
Two stages leak complementary halves of the same coefficient. The centred binomial sampler stores each one as a signed 16-bit two's-complement word, so the sign dominates the Hamming weight and is recovered almost without error — but the magnitude is not, and sign alone does not produce long error-free hint sets. The number-theoretic transform that runs immediately afterwards multiplies each coefficient by public twiddle factors, and that multiplication leaks the magnitude. Used together as hints in a primal lattice attack on ML-KEM-768, the estimated BKZ block size falls from 624 to 129, or 2^182.2 to 2^37.7 in the core-SVP model.

The control experiment is the part worth keeping. Feeding the same NTT code a near-uniform operand leaks its Hamming weight just as strongly and reveals almost nothing about its value — so what makes a coefficient extractable is how few values it can take, not how small it is.

The countermeasure follows from that observation. Store each sample v as ṽ = v + rq for random nonzero r, a different representative of the same residue class, so the NTT and everything downstream run unchanged. Sign leakage drops to the noise floor, NTT magnitude leakage falls 4.5×, and block size returns to 611 — about four bits of estimated security lost instead of more than 140 — for 937 bytes of firmware.

This is an unrefereed preprint, and the figures are lattice-model estimates from power measurements on one optimised implementation, not executed key recoveries.

glossary.definition: The module-lattice key-encapsulation mechanism published as FIPS 203 in August 2024, defined at three parameter sets and intended to replace classical key exchange against a future quantum computer.
The narrow, zero-centred distribution the secret coefficients are drawn from. Its purpose is that the values stay small, and that narrowness is exactly what makes them recoverable here.
A finite-field relative of the FFT that turns polynomial multiplication into pointwise multiplication. It runs on the secret right after sampling, which puts it inside the attack path.
The tuning parameter of the lattice-reduction algorithm used to price an attack. Running time grows exponentially in it, so β is the quantity security levels are actually quoted against.

items.title: Differentiating attention twice stops needing an N×N tensor
items.dek: Anthony Givans, Michael Crawshaw and Mingrui Liu published FlashBoB, an algorithm that takes a gradient through attention's own backward pass without ever building a sequence-by-sequence matrix, and ran it at 262,000 tokens on one A100 where existing exact code stops at 16,000.
items.why_it_matters: Anything that differentiates through a training step — meta-learning, hyperparameter optimisation, test-time training, second-order optimisers — needs the derivative of the backward pass, and that is exactly where the fused attention kernels stopped helping. FlashAttention avoids materialising the score matrix by recomputing tiles on the fly; the double backward had no equivalent, so implementations fell back to writing the full square intermediates to memory and then ran out of it. Restoring the tiling moves the ceiling on all of those methods from a context length nobody trains at to one people do.
items.background_md: Attention compares every token with every other, so the natural intermediate is an N × N matrix of scores for a sequence of length N. Writing that matrix out to high-bandwidth memory and reading it back is what makes long-context attention slow — the arithmetic is cheap beside the traffic. The standard remedy is never to build it: process the sequence in tiles small enough to sit in on-chip SRAM and recompute the scores during the backward pass rather than storing them. Cost is then counted in bytes moved rather than operations performed, which is why these algorithms are described by an I/O complexity.
items.deeper_md:
The structural claim is what makes the schedule possible: in the double backward of softmax attention, two row-wise scalars determine all of the outputs through affine transformations, so every N × N quantity can be rebuilt inside a tile instead of stored. That gives a two-pass schedule with bounded on-chip SRAM use and Θ(N²d²/M) traffic to high-bandwidth memory, for head dimension d and memory size M — which, inside the usual FlashAttention score-recomputation model, matches the large-cache lower bound inherited from exact forward attention.

Measured: exact backward-over-backward at N = 262K on a single A100 80GB, where PyTorch exact baselines fail by N = 16K, and up to 6.3× faster than FlashBack, the JAX/Pallas implementation Engstrom and Feldmann released for the same operation. That repository is worth reading alongside the paper, because it says plainly that softmax was the hard case — its sigmoid-attention double backward was already fast, while softmax needed the probability matrix reinstantiated several times.

Two things to hold lightly. The 6.3× is one baseline on one GPU generation. And the applications named for it — second-order optimisation, gradient-based memory, meta-learning — are ones whose payoff at long context is still an open research question rather than a settled win this kernel unlocks.

glossary.definition: Differentiating the backward pass itself, which is what any method optimising through a training step requires. It is a second derivative, and its intermediates are larger than the first pass's.
The small fast memory on the accelerator die and the large slow stacks beside it. Tiled kernels exist to keep working data in the first and cut round trips to the second.
Cost measured in bytes moved between memory levels rather than arithmetic operations performed — the right currency whenever a kernel is bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound.
Sequence length and per-head dimension. Attention's intermediates grow as N² while its parameters grow with d, which is why long context becomes a memory problem before it becomes a compute problem.

foundations.topic: Subthreshold swing and the 60 mV/decade limit
foundations.subtitle: The thermodynamic floor that ended voltage scaling — and the background to today's Pulse item claiming 15 mV/decade.
foundations.tldr: A transistor switches off by making carriers climb an energy barrier, and temperature spreads their energies out. At 300 kelvin that spread costs about 60 millivolts of gate voltage for every factor of ten you want the current to fall, no matter how the device is built. That number is why supply voltages stopped dropping around a volt, why leakage became a first-order design problem, and why every serious attempt to beat it has to change either where the carriers come from or how much of the gate voltage reaches the channel.

sections.heading: Where 60 millivolts comes from
sections.body_md:
Start with the thing a transistor actually does when it is off. Source electrons sit at one energy, the channel presents a barrier, and only the electrons in the high-energy tail of the thermal distribution get over it. That tail is exponential: the population above an energy falls by a factor of e for every kT of extra height, where k is Boltzmann's constant and T the absolute temperature.

Gate voltage lowers the barrier, so drain current rises exponentially with it. Put numbers on it. At 300 K the thermal voltage kT/q is about 25.9 millivolts. A factor of ten is ln(10) ≈ 2.303 of those, so the gate has to move 2.303 × 25.9 ≈ 59.6 millivolts to change the current tenfold.

That is the whole derivation. Nothing in it mentions gate length, oxide thickness, mobility or material. It is a statement about statistics at temperature, which is why shrinking a transistor never made it better.
sections.deeper_md: Two refinements worth having. First, the figure scales with absolute temperature, not with anything else: at 77 K the same arithmetic gives about 15 mV/dec, which is the real reason cryogenic CMOS is interesting and is exactly the direction today's Pulse item's device moves when cooled to 100 K. Second, 60 mV/dec is an idealisation even at the limit. Beckers, Jazaeri and Enz show that below a critical temperature the achievable swing stops following kT/q at all and saturates at a temperature-independent value set by the extent of the band tail — states smeared below the band edge by the finite periodicity of a real lattice, plus defects and disorder. The floor is thermal until it is not; then it is a materials-quality floor.

sections.heading: The body factor: why a real transistor is worse
sections.body_md:
A real MOSFET does not deliver all of its gate voltage to the channel surface. The gate capacitance and the depletion capacitance of the silicon below form a divider, so a change of one volt at the gate moves the surface potential by less than a volt. The subthreshold swing picks up exactly that divider as a multiplier: S = (kT/q)·ln(10)·(1 + C_dep/C_ox), usually written as S = 60·n mV/dec with n the body factor.

This is the part process engineering can attack, and the last twenty years of device architecture is largely the story of attacking it. Thinner and higher-permittivity gate dielectrics raise C_ox. Fully depleting the body — FD-SOI, then FinFET, then gate-all-around nanosheets — removes most of C_dep by leaving no undepleted silicon to hold the charge. Each step pushes n toward 1 and S toward the mid-60s.

And there it stops. Hu's MOS transistor chapter is worth reading for the full derivation, because the shape of the argument tells you where the remaining room is: none of it is in the 60.
sections.deeper_md: Bulk planar devices ran n around 1.3 to 1.5, which put practical swings near 80–90 mV/dec. Getting n to roughly 1.05 is a large engineering win and a small physics win: it buys maybe a 25% reduction in the gate swing needed per decade, once, and then the 60 stands alone. Note also what n does to the drain side. A high body factor means the surface potential is weakly controlled by the gate, which is the same condition that makes drain-induced barrier lowering severe — so swing and short-channel behaviour are two readings of one quantity, and an architecture that fixes one usually fixes the other.

sections.heading: What the floor costs: the power wall
sections.body_md:
Here is why a number about an off-state governs the whole chip. A logic gate has to be properly off and properly on, which means the gate voltage has to span several decades of current — call it five or six for a reasonable ratio between leakage and drive. At 60 millivolts per decade, that is already 300 to 360 millivolts of gate range spent before any overdrive, and overdrive is what actually delivers speed.

So supply voltage cannot fall below roughly that sum. Dynamic switching energy goes as CV², so a supply that will not fall is an energy per operation that will not fall either. That is the end of Dennard scaling stated in one line: transistors kept getting smaller and denser, and the energy each one costs to switch stopped following.

The alternative is to accept more leakage. Lower the threshold voltage and every decade you give up multiplies the static current of every one of the billions of off transistors on the die, all the time.
sections.deeper_md: The arithmetic to carry around: off-current rises by 10× for every S millivolts the threshold drops, so at S = 70 mV/dec, shaving 210 mV off V_th is a thousand-fold increase in static power. Modern designs respond by refusing to use one threshold — multi-V_th libraries put low-threshold, leaky, fast cells only on paths that failed timing and high-threshold cells everywhere else, and power gating switches whole blocks out of the supply rail. All of that is bookkeeping around a constant, and none of it moves the constant.

sections.heading: Escape route one: change where carriers come from
sections.body_md:
The 60 exists because injection is thermal. Remove the thermal tail from the injection process and the floor goes with it.

The tunnel FET does this by band-to-band tunnelling. Line the source's valence band up against the channel's conduction band and electrons cross through the forbidden gap; states above the source's valence band edge have nothing to tunnel into, so the high-energy Boltzmann tail is filtered out by the band structure itself. Swings well under 60 mV/dec follow directly.

The cold-source approach keeps normal thermionic injection but changes the contact material. Liu's simulations of transition-metal dichalcogenides such as NbX₂ and TaX₂ (X = S, Se, Te) use a source whose density of states falls away above the Fermi level, which truncates the same tail from the other side.

Both work, and both pay in the same currency. Ilatikhameneh and colleagues state the TFET problem plainly: low ON-current. Filtering out the energetic carriers filters out most of your drive.
sections.deeper_md: That trade is the reason steep-slope devices are benchmarked on a plot of swing against current density rather than on a single number: a device can be beautifully steep at a picoamp and useless at a milliamp. The tunnelling rate depends exponentially on the field at the junction, which is why the 2D TFET work emphasises tight gate control and thin bodies — and why Ilatikhameneh and colleagues find the material choice is not free either, since band gap, effective mass and source/drain doping all enter the ON-current through the same exponent.

sections.heading: Escape route two: amplify the gate
sections.body_md:
The second route leaves injection thermal and attacks the body factor instead. If S = 60·n and n = 1 + C_dep/C_ox, then a negative C_ox would give n below 1, and the surface would see more voltage swing than the gate supplies.

A ferroelectric can provide that. Biased in the region of its free-energy double well where polarisation falls as the applied field rises, its differential capacitance is negative; stack it above the oxide and the series combination amplifies. Today's Pulse item takes the idea one step further by amplifying the field that opens a bandgap in bilayer graphene rather than the field that fills a channel, which sidesteps the fact that the semiconductor's own capacitance moves as carriers arrive.

This is also where the field argues with itself. Kittl and co-workers hold that stabilising negative capacitance by matching it to an adjacent dielectric is "fundamentally flawed and unphysical", and that microscopic measurements show mixed ferroelectric domains rather than the single uniform low-polarisation state the models assume.
sections.deeper_md: The dispute is worth understanding precisely, because it is not about whether a measurement showed sub-60 behaviour. It is about what is being measured. A ferroelectric switching between domains transiently pushes charge in a way that can look like amplification in a quasi-static sweep, and a hysteretic device can report a steep swing on one direction of the sweep that it does not reproduce on the other. Kittl and co-workers do not claim stabilised negative capacitance is impossible — they say the capacitance-matching argument for it does not hold, and recommend looking at systems where the effect is actually feasible. So the caveat to attach to any NCFET number is not "some are skeptical" but a specific question: was the sweep hysteresis-free, and was the steepness reproducible in both directions?

sections.heading: How to read a sub-60 claim
sections.body_md:
Claims of sub-thermal switching appear regularly, and most of the work of assessing one is separating three different numbers that get quoted interchangeably.

First, point swing versus average swing. Cui and colleagues report InAlN/GaN transistors with 40 nanometre gates at an average of 30 mV/dec across three decades of drain current, and a minimum point-by-point value of 15 mV/dec. The minimum is the local slope at one bias; the average is the number that determines how much gate range you actually need. Quote the second.

Second, over how many decades. A swing quoted over one decade near the noise floor is nearly meaningless; three decades is a real claim.

Third, simulated or measured. Today's negative-capacitance item is entirely a model, and it says so — and it also states its own killer, an on/off ratio of about 10² where logic wants 10⁵. A steep slope that only runs over two decades of current has not solved the problem the 60 created; it has moved it.
sections.deeper_md: A fourth check, for any device with a ferroelectric or a charge-trapping layer in the stack: sweep both directions and look for hysteresis, and sweep at more than one rate. A genuine steady-state steep slope is rate-independent; a transient one is not. And a fifth, for anything cryogenic: compare against the correct floor for that temperature rather than against 60. At 77 K the thermal limit is about 15 mV/dec, so a 15 mV/dec result at 77 K is an ordinary transistor working exactly as expected, while the same number at 300 K is an extraordinary claim.

glossary.definition: The gate-voltage range below threshold where the channel is not inverted and current flows by diffusion of thermally excited carriers over the barrier. Current there is exponential in gate voltage, which is what makes a swing in millivolts-per-decade the natural unit.

Boltzmann's constant times absolute temperature divided by the electron charge — about 25.9 mV at 300 K. It is the natural voltage scale of every thermally activated process in a device, and everything in this piece is a multiple of it.

The gate voltage change that alters drain current tenfold, in mV/decade. Reported either as the minimum point-by-point slope or as an average over a stated number of decades; the two can differ by a factor of two and only the second predicts circuit behaviour.

The capacitive divider 1 + C_dep/C_ox between gate and channel surface, which multiplies the thermal limit: S = 60·n mV/dec at room temperature. Fully depleted architectures push n toward 1, and nothing in conventional CMOS pushes it below.

The drain current with the gate at zero volts — the leakage every off transistor on the die pays continuously. It rises tenfold for every S millivolts the threshold voltage is reduced, which is the direct link between swing and static power.

Carriers crossing from the valence band on one side of a junction into the conduction band on the other, through the forbidden gap rather than over a barrier. Because it requires aligned states, it truncates the thermal tail — and delivers far less current than thermionic injection.

States smeared into what should be the forbidden gap by the finite periodicity of a real crystal, plus defects and disorder. At deep-cryogenic temperatures the band tail, not kT/q, sets the achievable swing.

foundations.try_this: Three things, all doable this week and none needing a fab. First, do the derivation by hand: compute kT/q at 300 K, multiply by ln(10), and satisfy yourself that 59.6 mV/dec falls out of nothing but Boltzmann's constant and the electron charge — then redo it at 350 K and 250 K and note that the answer is strictly proportional to absolute temperature. Second, measure it in simulation with the open PDK the club already has: in ngspice with SKY130, sweep V_GS on an nFET from 0 V up past threshold at fixed V_DS, plot log₁₀(I_D) against V_GS, and take the inverse slope of the straight part — that is S. Re-run the same sweep with the temperature option set to 300 K and to 350 K, confirm S tracks T, then back out the body factor as n = S / (59.6 mV/dec × T/300 K); anything near 1.1 to 1.3 is a sane model. Third, read the abstract and transfer curves of arXiv:2005.08423 and work out for yourself why the authors report both 30 mV/dec and 15 mV/dec for the same device, and which of the two you would put in a circuit-level power budget. If you want the full textbook derivation alongside, Chapter 6 of Chenming Hu's *Modern Semiconductor Devices for Integrated Circuits* is the MOS transistor chapter and the PDF is free on his Berkeley page.
